I feel tension in my wrist when I play. How do I fix this?

Bertrand would say: don't fix it — notice it. The Perfect 4th is the foundation of power chords and the backbone of rock. Here you face the Tests — the fretboard seems impossibly complex.

Try this: The Five Neighborhoods

The tension you feel in your wrist is not a mistake. It's information. Your body is telling you where you are holding resistance. In Fret 6 (Approach to the Inmost Cave), we learn that See how music shows up on the guitar. The SHEARL protocol: See it, Hear it, Feel it.

Start with the Body Scan: sit with your guitar, close your eyes, and breathe into the tension. Don't push it away. Just acknowledge it. The release will come when the awareness is genuine.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

What is the ©PLING! method?

©PLING! stands for Pitch-Listen-Internalize-Note-Guitar. It is the neurological core of Bertrand's method.

Before you play a note on the guitar, you SING it first. This is not optional — it is the foundation. Your vocal tract wires directly to your auditory cortex. When you sing a pitch before playing it, you are building a neural bridge between your inner ear and your motor cortex.

The sequence:
1. Hear the pitch internally (audiation)
2. Sing it aloud
3. Find it on the guitar
4. Compare — did they match?

This is Fret 7 territory — the Ordeal. The tritone (√2:1) lives here, the most dissonant interval. ©PLING! teaches you to navigate dissonance with your voice as compass.

As Bertrand says: 'If you cannot sing it, you cannot play it.'

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

You are an instrument playing an instrument. Before you tune the wooden box, you must tune the biological one. The body is your first instrument — your fascia, your breath, your nervous system. Physic

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

Tell me the story of The Treatise That Named the Overtones.

It produces a cascade of overtones — an octave above, then a fifth, then another octave, then a major third — in diminishing brightness. The Perfect Fifth is the first non-octave overtone: ratio 3:2.

Rameau proved that the chord is not a human invention. It is a physical fact. The major triad exists inside every single vibrating string, waiting to be heard.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Minor 7th is the penultimate tension. The audience is not your enemy — it is a mirror reflecting your emotional truth.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

Tell me the story of Musica Enchiriadis.

The medieval Church did not ban the tritone because it sounded bad. They banned it because it sounded *unresolved* — and in a theology built on certainty, an unresolved sound was a theological problem.

But the ban created a paradox. By forbidding the tritone, the Church ensured that every musician in Europe knew exactly what it sounded like. The forbidden interval became the most recognized interval in Western music. Composers began hiding it in their work — not as defiance, but as expression. The tritone became the secret language of tension, longing, and the unsayable.

Every blues riff you have ever heard uses the tritone. Every dominant seventh chord contains it. The thing the Church feared most became the engine of all modern harmony.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

Tell me the story of De Vita Libri Tres.

In 1619, Johannes Kepler published *Harmonices Mundi* — "The Harmony of the World." In it, he made an extraordinary claim: the planets, as they orbit the sun at varying speeds, produce intervals that correspond to the Pythagorean ratios.

Saturn, the slowest, hums a low drone. Jupiter sings a major third above it. Mars, with its eccentric orbit, sweeps through a perfect fifth. Earth oscillates between mi and fa — a semitone — which Kepler interpreted as the Earth singing "misery" (*miseria*) and "famine" (*fames*).

Kepler was not being poetic. He was a mathematician. He derived his Third Law of Planetary Motion from this musical investigation. The math that describes how planets orbit is the same math that describes why a major chord sounds bright.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Minor 6th is bittersweet beauty. This is not about playing harder or faster. It is about playing with the absolute minimum necessary force.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

Tell me the story of Micrologus.

Guido's system did not stay in Italy. French cathedral schools adopted it within a generation. By the 12th century, Notre-Dame de Paris was training choirboys using the Guidonian Hand — and those choirboys grew up to become the first polyphonic composers in history.

The *École de Notre-Dame* — Léonin and Pérotin — stacked voices on top of each other for the first time, creating harmony where there had only been melody. They could do this because Guido had given them a reliable way to teach pitch. Without the hand, there would be no harmony. Without solfège, there would be no chord.

The Minor 3rd — the sound of melancholy, of depth — was born in these stone cathedrals, carried by the living voices of French choirboys who learned to sing by pointing at their own hands.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

What is the ©PLING! method?

©PLING! stands for Pitch-Listen-Internalize-Note-Guitar. It is the neurological core of Bertrand's method.

Before you play a note on the guitar, you SING it first. This is not optional — it is the foundation. Your vocal tract wires directly to your auditory cortex. When you sing a pitch before playing it, you are building a neural bridge between your inner ear and your motor cortex.

The sequence:
1. Hear the pitch internally (audiation)
2. Sing it aloud
3. Find it on the guitar
4. Compare — did they match?

This is Fret 7 territory — the Ordeal. The tritone (√2:1) lives here, the most dissonant interval. ©PLING! teaches you to navigate dissonance with your voice as compass.

As Bertrand says: 'If you cannot sing it, you cannot play it.'

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Minor 2nd is dissonance — the first friction. It is the moment you realize something is wrong with how you have been practicing.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Tritone is the exact midpoint of the octave. Maximum tension. Maximum dissonance. This is the Inmost Cave.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively

- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

Tell me the story of Music as Medicine.

In 1489, Marsilio Ficino — priest, philosopher, physician, and head of the Platonic Academy in Florence — published *De Vita Libri Tres* (Three Books on Life). In Book III, he made an extraordinary claim: specific musical intervals could heal specific ailments.

Ficino was not being metaphorical. He believed that the human body contained "spirits" — subtle vapors connecting body and soul — and that these spirits vibrated at frequencies that could be tuned by music, just as a string is tuned by tension. A melancholic patient needed solar intervals (bright major thirds, expansive sixths). A manic patient needed lunar intervals (cool minor seconds, grounding fourths).

Ficino played the lira da braccio for his patients in the gardens of Lorenzo de' Medici. Music was his prescription.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Minor 2nd is dissonance — the first friction. It is the moment you realize something is wrong with how you have been practicing.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Minor 2nd is dissonance — the first friction. It is the moment you realize something is wrong with how you have been practicing.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms

- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Perfect 4th is the foundation of power chords and the backbone of rock. Here you face the Tests — the fretboard seems impossibly complex.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

What is the ©PLING! method?

©PLING! stands for Pitch-Listen-Internalize-Note-Guitar. It is the neurological core of Bertrand's method.

Before you play a note on the guitar, you SING it first. This is not optional — it is the foundation. Your vocal tract wires directly to your auditory cortex. When you sing a pitch before playing it, you are building a neural bridge between your inner ear and your motor cortex.

The sequence:
1. Hear the pitch internally (audiation)
2. Sing it aloud
3. Find it on the guitar
4. Compare — did they match?

This is Fret 7 territory — the Ordeal. The tritone (√2:1) lives here, the most dissonant interval. ©PLING! teaches you to navigate dissonance with your voice as compass.

As Bertrand says: 'If you cannot sing it, you cannot play it.'

Every vibrating string is a tower of sound.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Tritone is the exact midpoint of the octave. Maximum tension. Maximum dissonance. This is the Inmost Cave.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

Tell me the story of Quatuor pour la fin du temps.

William Blake — poet, painter, visionary — wrote:

*To see a World in a Grain of Sand,
And a Heaven in a Wild Flower,
Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand,
And Eternity in an hour.*

The octave is Blake's grain of sand. It is the smallest complete cycle in music — one note returning to itself at double the frequency. Everything that will ever happen in music happens within this single span of twelve semitones. Every scale, every chord, every melody, every harmony is a subset of this one journey from root to octave.

You have traveled all twelve frets. You have met Pythagoras in his forge, Boethius in his cell, Guido with his hand raised, Debussy at his piano, Messiaen in his prison camp. The song was always the same song. The voice was always your voice.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Octave is the same note you started with — but vibrating at twice the frequency. You no longer play the guitar; the guitar plays through you.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

What is the ©PLING! method?

©PLING! stands for Pitch-Listen-Internalize-Note-Guitar. It is the neurological core of Bertrand's method.

Before you play a note on the guitar, you SING it first. This is not optional — it is the foundation. Your vocal tract wires directly to your auditory cortex. When you sing a pitch before playing it, you are building a neural bridge between your inner ear and your motor cortex.

The sequence:
1. Hear the pitch internally (audiation)
2. Sing it aloud
3. Find it on the guitar
4. Compare — did they match?

This is Fret 7 territory — the Ordeal. The tritone (√2:1) lives here, the most dissonant interval. ©PLING! teaches you to navigate dissonance with your voice as compass.

Tell me the story of Before the First Note.

In 12th-century Occitania — the south of France — a poet-musician called a troubadour would sit before his lute and do something radical: nothing. He would hold the silence. He believed the song was already present in the air, and that his first job was not to play it, but to listen for it.

The troubadours called their art the "living voice" — *voix vive*. Not music written on a page. Music breathed from a living body. They were the first to say: the voice comes before the note. The self comes before the song.

Tell me the story of Messe de Nostre Dame.

The guitar is tuned in fourths. This is not a design choice — it is a lesson built into the instrument's body.

Every time you move from one string to the next, you cross a Perfect Fourth. The fretboard is a grid of fourths. The shapes you learn — the chord voicings, the scale patterns, the arpeggios — are all consequences of this one tuning decision made centuries ago by French luthiers who inherited Pythagorean ratios from Boethius who inherited them from the Brotherhood.

You do not need to memorize this history. You are playing it. Every time your hand moves vertically across the strings, the 4:3 ratio moves through your fingers. The instrument is not a tool you use to make music. The instrument *is* the music, patiently teaching you its geometry every time you pick it up.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

Tell me the story of Harmonie Universelle.

The Perfect Fifth — 3:2 — is the most consonant interval after the octave. It is the sound of power chords, of open tunings, of resolution. It is the reward.

But here is the secret: the reward was always there. The 3:2 ratio existed in the string before you plucked it. The overtone was present before the fundamental sounded. The harmony was waiting inside the physics.

You did not earn the Perfect Fifth. You uncovered it. Every hour of practice, every scale, every fumbled chord change — none of it created the beauty. It was always there. Practice simply removed the obstacles between you and the sound that was already present.

This is the Supreme Ordeal's reward: the realization that you were never building something. You were clearing a path to something that already existed.

What is the ©PLING! method?

©PLING! stands for Pitch-Listen-Internalize-Note-Guitar. It is the neurological core of Bertrand's method.

Before you play a note on the guitar, you SING it first. This is not optional — it is the foundation. Your vocal tract wires directly to your auditory cortex. When you sing a pitch before playing it, you are building a neural bridge between your inner ear and your motor cortex.

The sequence:
1. Hear the pitch internally (audiation)
2. Sing it aloud
3. Find it on the guitar
4. Compare — did they match?

This is Fret 7 territory — the Ordeal. The tritone (√2:1) lives here, the most dissonant interval. ©PLING! teaches you to navigate dissonance with your voice as compass.

As Bertrand says: 'If you cannot sing it, you cannot play it.'

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

Tell me the story of The Rule of Silence.

In the school of Pythagoras, newcomers were not allowed to speak. For five years. The practice was called *echemythia* — the discipline of closed lips. You could listen. You could observe. This was not punishment. It was the first lesson: your mind's chatter is louder than any instrument. Until you can sit in silence without flinching, you cannot hear the ratios that hold the universe together. The 16:15 ratio — the Minor 2nd — is the smallest step. It begins with not speaking.

What is the ©PLING! method?

©PLING! stands for Pitch-Listen-Internalize-Note-Guitar. It is the neurological core of Bertrand's method.

Before you play a note on the guitar, you SING it first. This is not optional — it is the foundation. Your vocal tract wires directly to your auditory cortex. When you sing a pitch before playing it, you are building a neural bridge between your inner ear and your motor cortex.

The sequence:
1. Hear the pitch internally (audiation)
2. Sing it aloud
3. Find it on the guitar
4. Compare — did they match?

This is Fret 7 territory — the Ordeal. The tritone (√2:1) lives here, the most dissonant interval. ©PLING! teaches you to navigate dissonance with your voice as compass.

As Bertrand says: 'If you cannot sing it, you cannot play it.'

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

Tell me the story of The Concert at the End of Time.

On January 15, 1941, in Stalag VIII-A — a German prisoner-of-war camp in Görlitz, Silesia — Olivier Messiaen performed his *Quatuor pour la fin du temps* (Quartet for the End of Time) for an audience of 400 prisoners and guards.

The instruments were broken. The cello had only three strings. The clarinet was cracked. The piano keys stuck. Messiaen composed the piece in captivity, writing on the only paper he could find, in freezing barracks by candlelight.

Four hundred people — starving, freezing, imprisoned — listened in absolute silence. The music lasted fifty minutes. When it ended, no one moved. A guard later wrote: "Never before have I heard music of such purity."

The octave — 2:1 — is the return. The same note, doubled in frequency. You arrive where you began, but everything has changed.

Stalag VIII-A, Görlitz · January 15, 1941 · Quatuor pour la fin du temps

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Minor 7th is the penultimate tension. The audience is not your enemy — it is a mirror reflecting your emotional truth.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

- **Perfect 4th**: Five semitones. The tuning interval between most guitar strings. It is the backbone of the guitar\

These concepts connect to the Approach to the Inmost Cave stage of the Hero's Journey, where see how music shows up on the guitar. the shearl protocol: see it, hear it, feel it.

In 16th-century France, luthiers — the craftsmen who built lutes and early guitars — tuned their instruments in fourths: 4:3, 4:3, 4:3. This was not arbitrary. It was Pythagorean.

The Perfect Fourth is the most stable interval after the octave and the fifth. When you tune a guitar string to the one below it by matching the fifth fret, you are performing an act that connects you directly to the workshop of a French luthier 500 years ago, who was performing the same act using the same ratio that Pythagoras measured on his monochord 2,000 years before that.

The guitar is a quartal instrument. It is built on fourths. And every time you tune it, you are participating in an unbroken chain of acoustic tradition that spans three millennia.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

Tell me the story of Harmonie Universelle.

Around 1360, Guillaume de Machaut — a French poet, diplomat, and composer — created the *Messe de Nostre Dame* in Reims Cathedral. It was the first known complete polyphonic setting of the Ordinary of the Mass by a single composer.

Four voices — superius, contratenor, tenor, bassus — woven together in a structure so intricate that modern scholars still debate its mathematical architecture. Machaut used the Perfect Fourth extensively as a structural pillar, stacking voices at intervals that Pythagoras would have recognized instantly.

Machaut was not just a musician. He was a poet of courtly love, a survivor of the Black Plague, a canon of Reims Cathedral. He composed until his death at approximately 77 — in an era when life expectancy was 35. Music kept him alive.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

The Minor 3rd (three semitones) is the defining interval of minor chords and the blues scale. It carries the emotional weight of melancholy or tension.

On the guitar: The minor third spans three frets on a single string, or an offset diagonal across adjacent strings (depending on the tuning interval of the strings).

In the Pythagorean tradition: 6:5 — the ratio that gives minor chords their depth.

Physics: The first "minor" emotional colour. 6 vibrations for every 5.

What is the ©PLING! method?

Tell me the story of Utriusque Cosmi Historia.

In 523 CE, the Roman philosopher Boethius sat in a prison cell in Pavia, Italy, awaiting execution. He had served as consul to the Ostrogothic king Theodoric — and had been betrayed. He had lost everything: position, family, freedom.

In that cell, he wrote *The Consolation of Philosophy* — and its most enduring argument was about music. Boethius divided all music into three kinds: *musica mundana* (the music of the cosmos), *musica humana* (the harmony of body and soul), and *musica instrumentalis* (the sounds we actually play). The third kind — the one you hear with your ears — was the least important. The real music, he said, is the one holding you together right now.

Pavia, Italy · 523 CE · The last philosopher of Rome

"Music is so naturally united with us that we cannot be free from it even if we so desired." — Boethius, De Institutione Musica (c. 505 CE)

Tell me the story of De Institutione Musica.

After Rome fell, Boethius's book nearly vanished. What saved it — and with it, the entire Pythagorean theory of harmony — were Carolingian monks in French monasteries.

In the 9th century, under Charlemagne's patronage, monks in scriptoria across France began systematically copying every ancient text they could find. They copied Boethius's *De Institutione Musica* by hand, preserving the ratios, the monochord diagrams, the three-fold division of music. They also invented something new: *neumes* — the first written music notation in Western history, scratched above Latin hymn texts to remind singers where the melody went.

Without these French monks, the Pythagorean tradition would have died. The living voice needed a written memory.

France · 9th Century CE · The Carolingian Renaissance

"To write is to make a time capsule for the voice." — Attributed to Alcuin of York, advisor to Charlemagne

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Perfect 4th is the foundation of power chords and the backbone of rock. Here you face the Tests — the fretboard seems impossibly complex.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

Tell me the story of The Conductor Who Died for Music.

On January 8, 1687, Jean-Baptiste Lully — the most powerful musician in France, master of the king's music at Versailles — conducted a Te Deum celebrating Louis XIV's recovery from surgery. In that era, conductors kept time by striking a long wooden staff against the floor.

Lully struck his own foot with the staff. The wound became gangrenous. His doctors urged amputation. Lully refused — a dancer, he said, cannot lose a foot. He died two months later, at 54, of gangrene that spread from a conducting injury.

Lully died because he would not stop making music, even when music was killing him. The Minor 7th — one step from the octave, one step from home — is the interval of almost-there. Of commitment so total that retreat is impossible.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Minor 2nd is dissonance — the first friction. It is the moment you realize something is wrong with how you have been practicing.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

Tell me the story of The Body That Knows Itself.

In his treatise *De Anima* (On the Soul), Aristotle identified a sense that had no organ: *kinesthesis* — the body's awareness of its own position and movement. You do not need to look at your hand to know where it is. Something deeper than sight tells you.

Aristotle taught while walking — the Peripatetic method — because he believed that the body in motion thinks differently than the body at rest. His students played lyres while walking through the Lyceum gardens, learning that music is not produced by the fingers alone but by the entire body's relationship to gravity, balance, and breath.

The Minor 6th — eight semitones — is the interval of bittersweet searching. It is the sound of the body reaching for something it can almost feel.

Athens, Greece · c. 335 BCE · The Lyceum · De Anima

"The soul is in a way all existing things; for existing things are either sensible or thinkable." — Aristotle, De Anima, Book III

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

Stage fright is not fear of failure. It is fear of being seen.

The audience is a mirror. When you play for them, they do not hear your technique — they hear your emotional truth. If you are hiding, they hear hiding. If you are present, they hear presence. The Minor 7th — the penultimate tension — is the moment before you are fully exposed.

Lully could not stop conducting even when it was killing him because the music had become more real than his body. That is not recklessness. That is surrender. The ego dissolves when the music is more important than the musician.

The audience is not your enemy. They are the reason the song exists. Step into the light.

What is the ©PLING! method?

©PLING! stands for Pitch-Listen-Internalize-Note-Guitar. It is the neurological core of Bertrand's method.

Before you play a note on the guitar, you SING it first. This is not optional — it is the foundation. Your vocal tract wires directly to your auditory cortex. When you sing a pitch before playing it, you are building a neural bridge between your inner ear and your motor cortex.

The sequence:
1. Hear the pitch internally (audiation)
2. Sing it aloud
3. Find it on the guitar
4. Compare — did they match?

This is Fret 7 territory — the Ordeal. The tritone (√2:1) lives here, the most dissonant interval. ©PLING! teaches you to navigate dissonance with your voice as compass.

As Bertrand says: 'If you cannot sing it, you cannot play it.'
